DISCUSSION

Using DOOR analysis, an ASP intervention centered on T2Candida diagnosis resulted in an overall better clinical outcome compared to patients who were managed with an ASP strategy relying on blood culture diagnosis in this retrospective, observational cohort study. Consistent with other real-world studies, we found that T2Candida allowed for earlier identification of disease and faster time to appropriate antifungal therapy. Ultimately, prompt intervention likely led to the prevention of infectious complications and treatment failure resulting in an overall better clinical outcome among T2Candida/ASP patients. These findings are consistent with previous literature, which suggests that the use of rapid diagnostic tests in combination with ASP offers the greatest clinical benefit to patients with bloodstream infections, including those due to Candida species.

It is important to interpret these results within the context of the full ASP intervention at HFH that was aimed at optimizing outcomes among patients with candidemia. T2Candida was the cornerstone of a bundled approach that included empirical echinocandin therapy, administered in approximately half of patients. Notably, the frequency of empirical therapy deviated from the HFH ASP policy, which recommended the administration of an echinocandin at the time of T2Candida draw in all patients. Clinicians may have deemed patients to be sufficiently stable to delay therapy until T2Candida results were available, a real-world practice pattern that demonstrates the utility of T2Candida. The high negative predictive value of this diagnostic tool supports rapid discontinuation of empiric therapy if the T2Candida test returns negative results. The poor sensitivity of blood cultures does not allow for them to be used to justify withholding or discontinuing empirical antifungal therapy in high-risk patients. Thus, T2Candida serves as an important ASP tool to optimize antifungal prescribing. Although not evaluated in the present study, previous analyses have found reduced antifungal use associated with the implementation of T2Candida.

This study was not powered to detect a difference in 30-day all-cause mortality; however, the T2Candida/ASP group showed no association with reduced mortality, despite their lower baseline APACHE II scores and faster initiation of therapy. Previous literature suggests that early initiation of antifungal therapy is associated with reduced mortality in patients with candidemia. This paradigm may no longer strictly apply due to the increased comorbidity burden of critically ill patients, who may experience mortality from causes other than candidemia. Treatment practices have also evolved as echinocandins are now recommended as first-line agents in critically ill patients. The majority of patients included in this study received directed treatment with an echinocandin agent, which could perhaps offer some survival benefit regardless of baseline illness severity or slight delays in treatment initiation. Nevertheless, as illustrated by our findings, a reduction in time to therapy may confer other advantages, such as decreased infectious complications and treatment failure.

The use of the DOOR analysis in our study provided a more nuanced and detailed perspective of the overall clinical outcome of patients with candidemia. To our knowledge, no prior study has utilized a DOOR analysis to examine clinical outcomes associated with candidemia diagnosis or management. An exploratory DOOR analysis found that the use of the (1 3)-beta-d-glucan assay to direct initiation of antifungal therapy was more cost-effective compared to a hypothetical initiation of empirical therapy in all high-risk patients. However, this analysis only assessed the cost-effectiveness of initiating or withholding antifungal therapy based on subsequent blood culture results and did not evaluate the actual clinical outcome of the patient. Our DOOR analysis provides comprehensive information regarding the clinical status of critically ill patients with candidemia that is not available with bivariate end points alone.

Although it is possible that false positives were included within our data set, we expect this to be minimally contributing to our findings. Blood cultures have limited sensitivity for Candida spp., ranging from 28% to 58% in patients with postmortem-confirmed invasive candidiasis, depending on the extent of deep tissue infection. The detection of candidemia by T2MR technology depends upon the presence of an organism and does not detect circulating Candida DNA (DNA-emia), thus minimizing contamination-driven false positive specimens. In the original study of the T2MR system, it reproducibly detected five Candida species in whole blood, with a lower limit of detection of one colony-forming unit/milliliter. Additionally, it had a 98% positive agreement and 100% negative agreement in comparison to spiked blood samples. This was further confirmed in the clinical trial setting where T2Candida demonstrated 91.1% sensitivity compared to contrived specimens. Attesting to the greater sensitivity of T2Candida in comparison to blood cultures, several studies have demonstrated a higher level of sensitivity for detection in cases of intra-abdominal candidiasis with negative blood culture. Other studies of T2Candida that have analyzed T2Candida positive/blood culture-negative cases with clinical adjudication have identified probable or possible invasive candidiasis in other sites.

There are several limitations to this study. First, this was a retrospective analysis comparing candidemia ASP management strategies in two different healthcare systems. Although both are academic institutions serving an urban population within the metro Detroit area, there were significant baseline differences between groups. Moreover, the sample was not derived through random sampling given pragmatic limitations. We attempted to adjust for confounders utilizing IPTW, but there may be unmeasured covariates not accounted for in this adjustment. Second, there is currently no consensus DOOR definition for candidemia. We created the DOOR primary outcome for candidemia based on relevant end points modeled after DOOR components previously developed for bacterial bloodstream infections. However, the DOOR scale utilized herein has not been widely validated or standardized. Our DOOR components were developed collaboratively with our study team, but ideally, the development of a DOOR outcome should include even broader input from patients and clinicians from various practice settings. Next, there is a particular challenge in identifying persistent candidemia in HFH patients via T2Candida, as the ASP protocol discouraged repeat T2Candida testing. However, a similar frequency of patients at each site had a negative blood culture drawn within 120 h of the index blood culture/T2Candida test. Thus, there was a similar opportunity for detection of this outcome in both groups. Finally, it is possible patients with an initial test with indeterminate results were included if T2Candida was re-run with a positive result. However, the number of such occurrences is likely to be small and is not expected to significantly impact the study findings.

In conclusion, we developed and applied a novel DOOR analysis to assess the clinical impact of rapid molecular diagnosis within ASP. We found that the use of T2Candida as part of an ASP intervention was associated with an overall better clinical outcome in patients with candidemia, primarily driven by a reduction in infectious complications. Future analyses should continue to refine DOOR methodology in evaluating rapid molecular diagnostics on the outcome of candidemia, as well as to compare T2Candida practice strategies to further optimize patient outcomes and healthcare costs.

passages.text: Water stress enhances triacylglycerol accumulation via different mechanisms in wild-type and transgenic high-leaf oil tobacco
Abstract

Metabolically engineered high-leaf oil plants have been developed to meet the increasing demand for plant oils. Oil production of these plants under controlled conditions is promising; however, their performance under field-like conditions with abiotic stresses remains uncertain. In this study, wild-type (WT) and high-leaf oil (HLO) transgenic tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) plants were exposed to moderate and sustained water stress to mimic field conditions. The effects of water stress on biomass and lipid accumulation were investigated at the physiological, biochemical, and transcriptional levels. The presence of transgenes increased leaf triacylglycerol (TAG) levels in HLO plants by upregulating endogenous genes involved in lipid biosynthesis at the expense of biomass reduction, altered leaf lipid content and profile, and a decrease in unsaturation levels of membrane lipids compared to WT plants. Moreover, the biomass penalty in HLO plants could reduce canopy transpiration, contributing to their better performance under water-limited environments. Furthermore, WT and HLO plants exhibited enhanced TAG accumulation under water stress but via different mechanisms. In WT plants, water stress induced lipid remodeling, upregulated genes encoding phosphatidic acid phosphatase (PAP), diacylglycerol o-acyltransferase (DGAT2), and lipid droplet-associated proteins (LDAP1), but downregulated genes encoding Gly-Asp-Ser-Leu (GDSL) lipases. In contrast, HLO plants showed increased TAG accumulation primarily through upregulation of OLEOSINS and downregulation of GDSLs under water stress. In conclusion, moderate water stress promoted oil production in HLO plants, demonstrating the robustness of HLO technology for sustainable oil production in the field under water deficit conditions which may be more prevalent in the future due to climate change.
Moderate water stress enhances oil production in transgenic high-leaf oil tobacco plants, highlighting their potential for sustainable oil production under water-limited conditions.
Introduction

Plant oils are vital agricultural commodities due to their superior nutritional value as food and animal feed, and their potential as renewable biofuel sources. Global demand for plant oil is expected to double worldwide in the coming decades to meet growing food, feed, and industrial requirements. However, traditional oilseed crops primarily accumulate oils in the dominant form of triacylglycerols (TAG) in seeds, limiting production scalability. Metabolic engineering offers a promising solution by enhancing oil production in vegetative biomass. For instance, transgenic high-leaf oil (HLO) tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) plants can accumulate from 15% to 33% storage lipids, mainly in the form of TAG in leaves and stems of tobacco, by overexpressing a suite of lipid biosynthetic genes including WRINKLED1 (WRI1), DIACYLGLYCEROL ACYLTRANSFERASE 1 (DGAT1), OLEOSIN and LEAFY COTYLEDON2 (LEC2). Similar approaches have been explored in Arabidopsis, sugarcane, maize, and sorghum. Even though these results are promising for developing biomass-derived oil crops, understanding how HLO crops perform under natural environments with various abiotic stresses will be crucial for the practical deployment of this technology.

Water stress is a major constraint to plant growth and productivity, and occurs during different plant growth stages in diverse geographic regions. Water deficits lead to reduced biomass and yield by impacting essential plant processes, such as stomata closure, decreased turgor pressure, and accelerated leaf senescence. Stomata closure reduces leaf photosynthesis, while decreased turgor pressure impairs cell expansion and growth, negatively affecting overall plant development. Additionally, leaf senescence under water stress could reduce water loss and facilitate nutrient remobilization to sink organs but also diminish canopy size and the net rate of photosynthesis. Under drought conditions, the primary carbohydrate metabolism in leaves could be altered by converting starch into soluble sugars, such as glucose, fructose, and the raffinose family of oligosaccharides (RFOs), which contribute to osmoregulation and membrane stability.

Water stress also affects lipid metabolism in leaves, typically leading to an increase in neutral lipids like TAGs and a decrease in membrane polar lipids. In seed plants, TAGs accumulate in the cytoplasm as lipid droplets (LDs) and in the chloroplast as plastoglobules. Cytoplasmic LDs are spherical subcellular structures with a core of neutral lipids surrounded by a single layer of membrane lipids decorated with numerous integral and nonintegral proteins, such as OLEOSIN in seeds and LD-associated proteins (LDAPs) in vegetative tissues. Such proteins stabilize the LD surface and prevent LD aggregation, coalescence, and fusion, protecting TAG from degradation.

During leaf senescence, TAGs stored in LDs are broken down into their structural components, fatty acids (FAs) and glycerol, by a series of specific lipases (e.g. SUGARDEPENDENT1, SDP1). The resulting free FAs (FFAs) are mobilized into peroxisomes by the PEROXISOMAL TRASPORTER1 (PXA1) for degradation via the beta-oxidation pathway. On the other hand, abiotic stresses, such as drought and heat, can promote TAG levels. TAG can serve as an FA reservoir, which can be rapidly released to meet the cellular needs for energy metabolism and growth upon stress removal. The accumulation of leaf TAG under abiotic stresses is regulated by genes involved in TAG metabolism. For example, the gene encoding the chloroplastic enzyme acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACCase), which catalyzes the initial step of de novo FA synthesis, is upregulated under water stress in oat seedlings. Drought can also induce the expression of DGAT1 and PDAT2-A genes, which results in increased oil content in the roots of Tetraena mongolica and leaves of Camelina sativa. Furthermore, the genes encoding LDAPs, also known as small rubber particle proteins (SRPPs), which are important for LD formation and maintenance, are also strongly upregulated in response to abiotic stresses in various plant species.

Cell membranes, essential for stress perception and cellular integrity, undergo lipid modifications under environmental stress that influence membrane stability and fluidity. Phosphoglycerolipids such as phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) are the major components of nonplastidial cellular membranes, whereas plastidial membranes are mainly composed of phosphatidylglycerol (PG), monogalactosyldiacylglycerol (MGDG), and digalactosyldiacylglycerol (DGDG). MGDG and DGDG are the most abundant lipids in chloroplast membranes, regulating thylakoid membrane stability and integrity for photosynthetic electron transport. The DGDG/MGDG ratio determines membrane stability, affecting photosynthetic enzyme activity. Therefore, increasing the DGDG/MGDG ratio during water stress could be vital in membrane stabilization. Finally, a decline in unsaturated FA during water stress could be required to maintain the cellular membrane structure and function.

Water shortage hinders plant growth and productivity, but it is unknown how water stress disturbs the performance of HLO tobacco plants, an understanding of which is critical for deploying this technology in the field. This study aimed to investigate (i) the effects of transgenes in HLO on endogenous gene expression, oil accumulation and plant growth; (ii) how water stress affects the growth and oil accumulation in the HLO and WT plants; and (iii) the molecular and physiological mechanisms underlying the responses to water stress for both HLO and WT plants.
Results
Water stress led to biomass reduction in WT and HLO

Plants were subjected to water deficit treatment to investigate its effects on plant growth and oil production (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. S1). The gravimetric soil water content (thetag) decreased faster in WT than that in HLO, resulting in thetag reduction by 89.3% and 83.4% on 23 DAT for WT and HLO, respectively (Fig. 2A). Stomatal conductance (gs) of the 4th newly expanded leaf was monitored to assess the severity of water stress and guide the sample harvest (Fig. 2B). The first harvest (H1) was carried out 2 days after water stress treatment (DAT), with no differences observed in gs and soil water content between well-watered (WW) and water-stressed (WS). The second harvest (H2) was conducted at 16 DAT when the gs significantly (P < 0.01) decreased by almost 50% to the same level in WT and HLO under WS relative to those under WW (Fig. 2B). At 23 DAT, gs reached the lowest level of 57 mmol m-2 s-1 in WT and 125 mmol m-2 s-1 in HLO under water stress, prompting the third harvest (H3) (Fig. 2B). Subsequently, under WS, HLO maintained gs at 150-200 mmol m-2 s-1, while gs of WT steadily increased up to 300 mmol m-2 s-1 by the end of the treatment (37 DAT), when the final harvest (H4) was completed.

One replicate for each genotype under well-watered (WW), mean +- SE (n = 2) was shown for each genotype under and water-stressed (WS) condition. B) Stomatal conductance of the 4th newly expanded leaf, mean +- SE (n = 4) is shown for each genotype under WW and WS conditions. H1, 1st harvest; H2, 2nd harvest; H3, 3rd harvest; H4, 4th harvest.

Water stress significantly (P < 0.01) reduced plant dry weight by 29% in WT, compared to that under WW treatment at H3 (Fig. 2C). This reduction was due to a 28% and 32% decrease in leaf and stem/flowers DW, respectively. At H4, sustained water stress significantly (P < 0.01) reduced biomass accumulation of both genotypes but to a different extent. The total biomass of WT decreased by 52% (47% in leaf dry weight; 57% in stem and pod dry weight) under WS versus WW conditions, while that of HLO was reduced by 29% (24% in leaf dry weight; 35% in stem and pod dry weight) (Fig. 2C). Ultimately, there was no significant difference in total biomass between WT and HLO plants at H4. Throughout the whole growth period, the total biomass of HLO plants ranged from 54% to 65% of WT under WW, with leaf dry weight consistently between 55% and 69% of WT (Fig. 2C). Previous research observed similar results for plants grown under controlled environments. The smaller size of HLO plants likely resulted in a lower canopy transpiration rate, which may explain why HLO plants showed a relatively slower decline in thetag from H1 to H3. As a result, biomass accumulation in the HLO plants was less affected by water stress than in the WT plants.
Water stress enhanced TAG accumulation

The total TAG and TFA content were quantified in leaves of different ages to evaluate the effects of water stress on oil content when there were significant differences in biomass and gs for either genotype at H3 and H4. The transgenes were found to increase TAG levels from 134- to 279-fold depending on growth stage and leaf age compared to WT under WW at H3 and H4 (Fig. 3, A and B). Under WS, TAG significantly (P < 0.01) increased by 44% and 61% in the old and mature leaves of HLO, respectively, compared to WW at H3. In contrast, WS led to a 2.0-fold and 2.2-fold increase in TAG in the mature and young leaves of WT, respectively (Fig. 3A). The TFA content in HLO mirrored TAG accumulation trends, showing a significant (P < 0.05) increase of 34% in the mature leaf under WS, whereas TFA levels in WT remained unchanged (Fig. 3C). At H4, prolonged water stress significantly (P < 0.05) enhanced TAG and TFA accumulation in young leaves of HLO by 23% and 30%, respectively (Fig. 3, B and D). Tissue samples from mature leaves at H3, when both lines exhibited significant TAG increases, were utilized for subsequent analyses to explore both ongoing and potentially stabilizing processes related to TAG accumulation in the leaves.

Triacylglycerol (TAG) and total fatty acid (TFA) of WT (wild-type) and HLO (high-leaf oil) leaves under well-watered (WW) and water-stressed (WS) conditions at H3 (3rd harvest, 23 days after water stress treatment) and H4 (4th harvest, 37 days after water stress treatment). A) TAG content at H3; B) TAG content at H4; C) TFA content at H3; D) TFA content at H4. Bars are means +- SE (n = 3 or 4); asterisks indicated statistically significant differences using student's t-test (* P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01) between WW and WS for each genotype; only the comparisons with significant differences are indicated in the figure; all the comparisons between WT and HLO under WW conditions are significantly different.
Water stress induced changes in carbon partitioning

To assess how water stress affected carbon partitioning which might contribute to TAG increase, total carbon (C), soluble sugars, and starch content were measured. At H3, total C (on a dry weight basis) was marginally yet significantly (P < 0.01) lower in WT, whereas it remained unaffected in HLO (Fig. 4A). Water limitation also resulted in a lower starch content in both genotypes, with WT experiencing a significant (P < 0.01) decrease of nearly 80% (Fig. 4B). Under the WS condition, soluble sugar content showed an increasing trend for both WT and HLO, but a significant (P < 0.01) increase in soluble sugars was observed only in HLO by 17.2% (Fig. 4C). Compared to WT, HLO plants showed significantly higher total C (4%, P < 0.01), but lower soluble sugar (22%, P < 0.05).

Carbon partitioning of mature leaves in WT (wild-type) and HLO (high-leaf oil) plants under well-watered (WW) treatment and water-stressed (WS) treatment at H3 (3rd harvest, 23 days after water stress treatment). A) Total carbon; B) starch; C) soluble sugar. Bars are means +- SE (n = 3 or 4), and asterisks indicated statistically significant differences using student's t-test (* P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01) between WW and WS for each genotype, or between WT and HLO under WW; only the comparisons with significant differences are indicated.
Water stress altered the fatty acids profiles and composition of polar lipids

Fatty acids (FAs), with different carbon chain lengths and unsaturation degrees, are the key building blocks of glycerolipids. Fatty acids showed distinct alterations in TAG profiles of WT and HLO under WS. In WT plants, palmitic acid (PA, C16:0), stearic acid (SA, C18:0), and linoleic acid (LA, C18:2Delta9,12) were significantly (P < 0.01) reduced by 50%, 61%, and 27%, respectively, while alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, C18:3Delta9,12,15) and hexadecatrienoic acid (HTA, C16:3Delta7,10,13) increased dramatically (P < 0.01) by 1.2-fold and 11.7-fold under WS, respectively. In contrast, HLO plants exhibited significant increases in palmitoleic acid (POA, C16:1Delta9), oleic acid (OA, C18:1Delta9), and cis-vaccenic acid (VA, C18:1Delta11) by 35% (P < 0.05), 32% (P < 0.01), and 32% (P < 0.01), respectively, while LA decreased by 27% (P < 0.05) (Fig. 5A). Nevertheless, the FA profile in TFA pool was altered by water stress mainly in HLO. Both HTA and ALA, the trienoic fatty acids, significantly (P < 0.01) decreased by 38% and 36%, respectively, whereas the relatively minor unsaturated FAs, such as POA, OA, and VA were significantly (P < 0.01) increased by 50%, 58%, and 41% respectively (Fig. 5B). Meanwhile, significant changes were observed in the TAG and TFA fatty acid profiles of HLO plants compared to WT. Specifically, in the TAG fatty acid profile, POA, OA, VA, and LA significantly (P < 0.01 or 0.05) increased, with significant (P < 0.01) decreases in ALA (Fig. 5A). Similarly, the TFA profile showed significant (P < 0.01) increases in PA, OA, VA, and LA, but significant (P < 0.01) decreases in ALA (Fig. 5B).

A) TAG fatty acid profile. B) TFA fatty acid profile. Bars are means +- SE (n = 3 or 4), and asterisks indicated statistically significant differences using student's t-test (* P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01) between WW and WS for each genotype, or between WT and HLO under WW; only the comparisons with significant differences are indicated.

Meanwhile, the profiles of polar lipids such as phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylglycerol (PG), monogalactosyldiacylglycerol (MGDG), and digalactosyldiacylglycerol (DGDG), were analyzed using LC-MS. In WT plants under WS, there was a notable decrease in the content of these polar lipids compared to WW conditions, particularly MGDG and DGDG which decreased significantly (P < 0.05) by 70% and 49%, respectively (Fig. 6A). In contrast, HLO plants showed nonsignificant changes for the polar lipids quantified under WS. Furthermore, the DGDG/MGDG ratio increased significantly (P < 0.05) by 45% and 13% in WT and HLO under WS, respectively (Fig. 6B). On the other hand, the HLO plants showed significantly higher levels of PC compared to WT under both WW and WS conditions (Fig. 6A).

A) Polar lipids including PC, PE, PG, MGDG, and DGDG in WT and HLO under WW and WS. B) DGDG/MGDG ratio in WT and HLO under WW and WS. Bars are means +- SE (n = 3 or 4), asterisks indicated statistically significant differences using student's t-test (* P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01) between WW and WS for each genotype, or between WT and HLO under WW; only the comparisons with significant differences are indicated.
Genes involved in lipid metabolism were upregulated in HLO plants

To explore the influence of co-expressing WRI1, DGAT1, LEC2, and Sesamum indicum OLEOSIN on endogenous gene expression of tobacco, the global gene expression differences between WT and HLO were evaluated by transcriptomic analysis under WW and WS from mature leaves collected at H3, respectively. There were 2,110 genes upregulated, and 1,694 genes downregulated in the HLO plants compared to the WT under WW (Supplementary Fig. S2A). Despite the growth conditions, there were 1,441 genes constitutively upregulated and 701 genes downregulated in HLO compared to the WT, with a total of 1,694 and 1,622 genes downregulated in HLO vs WT under WW and WS, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S2B).

To investigate which metabolisms the above differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between WT and HLO are involved in, the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) term enrichment for DEGs was conducted (Fig. 7, A and B). The upregulated genes under WW and WS were enriched in KEGG terms mainly involved in lipid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and energy metabolism, while the downregulated genes functioned in lipid metabolism, carbon metabolism, and signal transduction (Fig. 7, A and B and Supplementary Fig. S2, C and D). Multiple pathways involved in lipid metabolism were prominently overrepresented in HLO plants under WW and WS conditions.

KEGG enrichment of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between WT (wild-type) and HLO (high-leaf oil) plants under well-watered (WW) conditions in mature leaves at H3 (3rd harvest, 23 days after water stress treatment). A) KEGG enrichment of upregulated DEGs between WT and HLO under WW; B) KEGG enrichment of downregulated DEGs between WT and HLO under WW. Yellow frames indicate set of genes involved in lipid metabolism pathways while those in blue are for carbohydrate metabolism.

Furthermore, a systematic analysis of genes involved in different pathways of lipid metabolism was undertaken between WT and HLO under WW (Fig. 8, A to D and Supplementary Table S1). The results indicated significant upregulation of genes encoding acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACCase), malonyl-CoA-ACP transacylase (MCMT), ketoacyl-ACP synthase III (KASIII), ketoacyl-ACP synthase I (KASI), 3-oxoacyl ACP reductase (KAR), enoyl-ACP reductase (ER), stearoyl-ACP desaturase (SAD), ketoacyl-ACP synthase II (KASII), hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase (HAD), fatty acyl-ACP thioesterase A (FATA), omega-6 fatty acid desaturase (FAD6), and long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 9 (LACS9) involved in de novo fatty acid biosynthesis (Fig. 8A and Supplementary Table S1). In addition, genes related to galactolipid biosynthesis in the chloroplast, such as GLYCEROL-3-PHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE (G3PDH), DGDG SYNTHASE 1 (DGD1), and PLASTOGLOBULAR PROTEIN 18 (PG18) were significantly upregulated (Fig. 8A and Supplementary Table S1). Similarly, genes participating in TAG assembly i.e. ACYL-COA-BINDING DOMAIN-CONTAINING PROTEIN (ACBP), GLYCEROL-3-PHOSPHATE ACYLTRANSFERASE 9 (GPAT9), LYSOPHOSPHATIDIC ACID ACYLTRANSFERASE (LPAAT), DGAT1, DGAT2, PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE:DIACYLGLYCEROL CHOLINEPHOSPHOTRANSFERASE (ROD1), (omega6)-DESATURASE (FAD2), (omega3)-DESATURASE (FAD3), PHOSPHOLIPID:DIACYLGLYCEROL ACYLTRANSFERASE 1 (PDAT1), PDAT2, PHOSPHOLIPASE A2 (PLA2), PHOSPHOLIPASE D (PLD), and PHOSPHOLIPASE C (PLC), as well as lipid droplet biogenesis i.e. OLEOSIN, LDAP, and LDAP-INTERACTING PROTEIN (LDIP), were significantly upregulated (Fig. 8, B and C and Supplementary Table S1). In contrast, the expression levels of most GDSL and MAGL genes involved TAG degradation were significantly downregulated, while genes involved in beta-oxidation i.e. PEROXISOMAL 3-KETOACYL-COA THIOLASE (PKT), and acyl-CoA OXIDASE (ACX) were significantly upregulated (Fig. 8D and Supplementary Table S1). Surprisingly, the expression of the HLO transgenes did not affect the transcription levels of the endogenous LEC2 and WRI1 under WW, but significantly increased that of MYB3, FUS3, and LEC1 in HLO (Fig. 9).

Mechanisms underlying TAG accumulation in response to water stress differed between WT and HLO

Analyses of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were performed for both genotypes to reveal the mechanism underlying the TAG accumulation during water stress at H3. Compared to the WW condition, 1,308 genes of WT and 572 genes of HLO were upregulated (Supplementary Fig. S3A), and 2,378 genes of WT and 721 genes of HLO were downregulated under WS, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S3B). The mechanism underlying the TAG accumulation in WT and HLO in response to WS was analyzed by comparing genes involved in different pathways of TAG metabolism as above (Fig. 8, A to D and Supplementary Table S1).

The gene Nitab4.5_0000469g0180 encoding ACCase, an important enzyme involved in de novo FA synthesis showed increased expression level in WT under WS (Fig. 8A). Similarly, two genes encoding TAG synthetic enzymes located in ER were upregulated in WT, including PAP (Nitab4.5_0000136g0260) and DGAT2 (Nitab4.5_0003141g0040) genes (Fig. 8B). In addition, genes encoding membrane-bound fatty acid desaturases FAD2, FAD3 and FAD8 significantly decreased in WT under WS (Fig. 8, A and B). Significantly, genes encoding proteins required for LD packaging, such as LDAP1 genes (Nitab4.5_0000060g0050; Nitab4.5_0001404g0050), were significantly upregulated under WS (Fig. 8C and Supplementary Table S1). Meanwhile, the expression of LDIP significantly increased under WS (Fig. 8C and Supplementary Table S1). Furthermore, WS resulted in a contrasting response in the expression of genes encoding phospholipases, with upregulated genes encoding PLD, a nonsignificant change of genes encoding PLC, but downregulation of genes encoding PLA2 (Fig. 8B). Besides, the genes encoding lipases involved in TAG degradation responded to water stress differently: two genes encoding GDSL lipase (GLIP) and three genes encoding monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) were upregulated, but most of the genes encoding GDSLs showed a reduction in expression level under the WS condition. Finally, the expression level of ACX and PKT, which participate in the beta-oxidation of fatty acids in the peroxisome, increased under WS (Fig. 8D).

On the other hand, most of the genes involved in de novo FA synthesis and TAG assembly in HLO plants were not significantly affected by water stress except for PDAT. Interestingly, PDAT1 was downregulated, whereas PDAT2 was upregulated under WS. Furthermore, among the 7 genes encoding oleosin proteins expressed in HLO, 3 genes were significantly upregulated, including 1 OLEOSIN1 (Nitab4.5_0002206g0060) and 2 OLEOSIN5 (Nitab4.5_0002624g0010 and Nitab4.5_0002682g0100) under WS (Fig. 8C). Meanwhile, genes encoding phospholipases (i.e. PLD, PLC, and PLA2 genes) and TAG lipase (i.e. GDSLs genes) responded to water stress similarly to WT (Fig. 8, B and C, and Supplementary Table S1). However, in HLO plants, water stress did not affect the expression of genes encoding lipases (i.e. SDP1 and MAGL) involved in the TAG degradation, nor did it affect ACX and PKT involved in beta-oxidation of fatty acids.

Finally, the genes involved in galactolipids biosynthesis in chloroplasts were not significantly affected by water stress for HLO except for GLYCEROL-3-PHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE (G3PDH), which was downregulated (Fig. 8A). This contrasts with WT, where genes encoding glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase 4 (GPAT4), galactolipid synthase 1 (MGD1), and DGD1 were all downregulated (Fig. 8A). On the other hand, lower expressions of genes involved in fatty acid and acyl-CoA transport, such as ATP-BINDING CASSETTE TRANSPORTER (ABCA) and ACBP, were observed under WS than in WW in both genotypes (Fig. 8, A and B).

In this study, most of the endogenous transcription factors (TFs), like WRI1, LEC2, FUS3, MYB73, and LEC1 that had been the focus previously to upregulate oil accumulation, were upregulated under WS in WT. For example, there were 1 WRI1 gene, 3 LEC2 genes, 3 MYB73 genes, and 7 LEC1 genes that were significantly upregulated under WS (Fig. 9). However, for HLO, only 2 LEC1 genes showed higher expression levels under WS compared to those under WW (Fig. 9).
Discussion
HLO plants maintained high oil production and performed better under water stress conditions

Water stress enhanced TAG accumulation in tobacco leaves, which is consistent with previous research on oats and Arabidopsis. The results also showed that the HLO plants could maintain high-leaf TAG levels under water-limited conditions. The estimated oil production per plant in HLO increased by 38.2% at H3 but decreased by 11.3% under WS at H4 compared to oil production under WW. These findings suggest that moderate water stress (i.e. at H3) could promote oil production in HLO plants, and maintaining a high level of oil accumulation is still possible under longer durations of water stress (i.e. at H4). Moreover, the high level of oil accumulation in HLO plants resulted in a biomass penalty, leading to a potential reduction in canopy transpiration (Fig. 2C). The reduced canopy transpiration could explain the higher soil thetag observed in the bins with HLO plants under WS compared to those with WT plants (i.e. the mean soil thetag of WT was 51% to 65% of that in HLO between H2 (14 DAT) and H3 (23 DAT) under WS, Fig. 2A). Therefore, the less water requirement of the HLO plants could explain the smaller biomass reduction under water stress compared to WT plants. Despite the reduced biomass yield potential of the HLO plants, this study demonstrated the efficacy of HLO technology for oil production in the vegetative tissue of tobacco under field-like conditions with moderate to severe water deficit.

TAG accumulation in plant vegetative tissues is one of the responses to water stress, and its content is positively related to plant performance under such conditions. TAG accumulation during water stress could sequester harmful FFAs generated during membrane degradation or remodeling to maintain membrane integrity. Interestingly, leaf TAG content increased in both HLO and WT under WS despite the adverse effects on biomass (Figs. 2C and 3A). Compared to WT, HLO plants showed 44 to 288 times higher TAG content (Fig. 3, A and B). The potential role of the increased TAG in mitigating the negative effects of water stress in this study requires further investigation.

Plants adjust the unsaturation level of FAs in membrane lipids as an adaptive strategy to ameliorate the detrimental effects of abiotic stress. Water stress elevates leaf temperature, which consequently leads to higher membrane fluidity. Therefore, reducing the degree of unsaturation under drought is likely another way to maintain optimal membrane fluidity and integrity. In this study, WT plants under WS showed reduction of ALA-containing MGDG and DGDG (34:6 and 36:6) molecular species (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. S4). In addition, the expression level of genes encoding plastidial omega3-desaturase (FAD8), responsible for enriching chloroplast membrane lipids with trienoic fatty acids, was decreased in WT under WS (Fig. 8A). In contrast, HLO plants maintained a consistently lower proportion of ALA-containing MGDG (34:6) and DGDG (36:6) even under WW, with similar level observed under WS (Supplementary Fig. S4). This suggests that the intrinsic lower degree of membrane lipid unsaturation in HLO may sustain membrane fluidity for optimal chloroplast function during water stress conditions.

In addition, the results showed opposite effects of leaf age on TAG accumulation in WT and HLO at H3. Specifically, under WS, TAG significantly accumulated in the younger leaves of WT, while the older leaves of HLO condition exhibited higher TAG content (Fig. 3A). This contrast may be attributed to accelerated TAG degradation caused by the aggravated leaf senescence in older leaves of WT under WS. However, the overexpression of LEC2 in HLO was driven by the Arabidopsis thaliana SAG12 senescence-specific promoter, resulting in higher expression in the older leaves. Consequently, the senescence-inducible expression of the transgenes in HLO plants could therefore activate genes involved in FA and TAG synthesis, and assist indirectly in further stabilizing TAG-containing LDs via upregulation of endogenous oil bodies or LDAPs, ultimately leading to a markedly higher TAG level in the older leaves of HLO under WS. Meanwhile, HLO plants showed relatively lower gs than WT plants at the end of the experiment under WW. In this study, the gs was measured on the newly and fully expanded leaves (i.e. always the fourth leaf from the top on the main stem). The leaf gs of HLO plants under WW conditions were 35% lower than that of WT plants at the end of the experiment (H4, Fig. 2). This reduction in gs is likely the results of an increased senescence in the leaves of the HLO plants compared to WT. HLO plants had more secondary branches and newly emerged leaves under WW than WT plants (Supplementary Table S2 and Supplementary Fig. S6). The newly emerged leaves could act as an additional carbon sink and accelerate the onset of senescence in the main stem leaves at H4. The other evidence of ontogenetic differences between main stem leaves of HLO and WT at H4 is the overall higher TAG levels observed in HLO compared to H3, and similar TAG levels across young, mature, and old leaves (Fig. 3, A and B). The relationship between TAG increase and leaf senescence is a consequence of the senescence-inducible expression of transgenes in HLO. Thus, it is plausible that the leaves of HLO plants used for measuring gs at H4 were at a more advanced stage of senescence, which could lead to declining gs under WW at H4. This conclusion is supported by higher measured values of gs in younger (top) leaves than in older (bottom) leaves in tobacco.
Carbon partitioning changed under water stress

Total C as a percentage of dry weight was higher in HLO plants than in WT under WW conditions (Fig. 4A). This could be explained by the fact that the HLO plants accumulated a large amount of TAG in the leaf and showed a trade-off in plant growth due to competition for carbon and key metabolic precursors. The allocation of carbon fixed by photosynthesis involves partitioning between sucrose in the cytoplasm and starch in the chloroplasts. Water stress reduced stomatal conductance, thereby affecting carbon assimilation (Figs. 2A and 4A). Interestingly, despite water stress, HLO plants maintained their total carbon content, showing a notable reduction in starch and a significant increase in soluble sugars (Fig. 4, A to C). This was consistent with previous research indicating that starch was remobilized into sucrose during altered carbon partitioning, leading to an increase of soluble sugar. This resource mobilization is a likely strategy to adapt to water stress because sugars can act as both osmoprotectants and an energy source for plant cells. Meanwhile, the soluble sugars under water stress trigger the production of specific ROS scavengers.

In contrast, the WT plants showed a significant reduction in total C and starch content under WS (Fig. 4, A and B). The reduction in total carbon and starch could be due to decreased photosynthetic capacity resulting from stomatal closure. Accordingly, a reduction in the expression level of genes involved in starch synthesis (i.e. APL and STS genes) and an increase in the expression of genes encoding starch degradation (i.e. AMY and BAM genes) were observed under WS in both genotypes (Supplementary Fig. S5). Moreover, the expression levels of genes involved in sucrose synthesis (i.e. GOLS, RFS2, AGAL, and SUS genes) were enhanced under WS in both genotypes (Supplementary Fig. S5). These results indicated that higher glucose levels could be available for glycolysis and FA synthesis under WS, which would be beneficial for the TAG accumulation and drought adaptation for WT and HLO plants.
Lipid remodeling occurred in WT under water stress but not in HLO

The remodeling and turnover of photosynthetic membrane lipids have been considered as an effective adapting strategy to accommodate and acquire tolerance to abiotic stresses. In this study, water stress provoked a decline in membrane lipids (i.e. PG, MGDG, and DGDG) in both genotypes, but it was more severe in WT (Fig. 6). On the other hand, the expression of PLASTOGLOBULAR PROTEIN 18 (PG18), a structural protein of plastoglobuli, was significantly upregulated in WT under WS (Fig. 8A). Plastoglobules which store neutral lipids in chloroplasts, are highly dynamic in size and shape, and play an important role in mobilizing lipids to form the thylakoid membrane and participating in the adaptation processes under abiotic stresses. Thus, these results suggested that lipid remodeling may occur in WT under WS, potentially involving increased plastoglobuli at the expense of membrane lipids like PG, MGDG, and DGDG. The observed higher DGDG/MGDG ratio in WT and HLO under WS had been reported to stabilize and maintain bilayer structure and protect chloroplasts from water stress-induced damages. However, the membrane lipids and the gene encoding PG18 were less affected by water stress in HLO than WT, indicating that lipid remodeling may not be the major event in HLO under WS.
Effects of transgenes on TAG synthesis of HLO plants under well-watered conditions

The leaf TAG content of HLO plants was 138-245 higher than WT under WW. The TAG accumulated in HLO plants was mainly through upregulating most of the genes involved in TAG synthesis, i.e. de novo fatty acid synthesis and TAG assembly, and lipid droplet biogenesis, but downregulating genes involved in TAG degradation (Fig. 8). Besides, the PC level in HLO was significantly higher than that in WT (Fig. 6A), which might provide more acyl editing according to for PC-derived DAG and/or TAG synthesis. It was supported by upregulated PDAT1 and PDAT2 in HLO plants compared to WT (Fig. 8B). The TAG enhancement in HLO plants may also be due to the upregulation of transcription factors such as MYB73, FUS3, and LEC1 (Fig. 9). Previous studies indicated that overexpression of LEC2 and/or LEC1 promoted oil accumulation in seeds of Arabidopsis, canola, and maize; Additionally, overexpression of FUS3 had been shown to increase the TAG accumulation in Arabidopsis and tobacco BY2 cells. Furthermore, overexpression of soybean GmMYB73 in Arabidopsis improved oil accumulation by enhancing PLDalpha1 expression. Similarly, in this study, elevated PLDs expression was noted in HLO plants compared to WT.

However, despite the enhancement, the TAG levels (~12.0%) of HLO plants observed were lower than previously reported, which could reach up to 29.8% TAG at the seed-setting stage. This discrepancy might be attributed to differences in growth conditions between experiments affecting nitrogen uptake and utilization. The results from another experiment that assessed the effect of varying nitrogen levels on oil production showed a negative relationship between nitrogen level and TAG accumulation (J. Zhang, T. Vanhercke, X.R. Zhou, G.M. Estavillo, unpublished data). In the current study, soil in a one cubic meter bin containing 3 to 12 plants was supplemented with 669 g Aboska fertilizer. The nitrogen amount was substantially higher than that was available for each plant in 4L pot used in the previous published study. This disparity in fertilizer application may explain the observed lower TAG levels compared to previous findings.
Enhancement of TAG accumulation under water stress via different mechanisms in WT and HLO plants

The mechanisms driving enhanced TAG accumulation differed between WT and HLO plants. The genes encoding key enzymes, such as PAP and DGAT involved in TAG biosynthesis from glycerol-3-phosphate and acyl-CoA via the Kennedy pathway, were upregulated under WS conditions, leading to elevated TAG levels in WT. Additionally, LDAP and LDIP play important roles in LDs biogenesis: LDAPs are abundant LD coat proteins in nonseed tissues and play important roles in both the formation and function of LDs; LDIP modulates both LD size and cellular neutral lipid homeostasis in both leaves and seeds. However, LDAPs are positively but LDIP is negatively correlated with the TAG accumulation. In this study, 2 LDAP1 genes and 1 LDIP gene were significantly upregulated in WT under WS. While the expression level of LDAP1 was relatively higher compared to that of LDIP. Thus, LDAP1 may be the dominant gene functioning in LD packaging other than LDIP. TAG degradation is catalyzed by a series of lipases. GDSL lipases are a recently discovered subclass of lipolytic enzymes involved in TAG degradation. For instance, overexpression of GDSL genes deceased seed oil content in Brassica napus. In this study, the genes from the GDSL family were mostly downregulated, especially Nitab4.5_0000202g0020 with 61.7% decreased expression under WS compared to that under WW conditions. Collectively, the TAG degradation could be decreased in WT under WS.

In HLO plants, water stress-induced TAG accumulation primarily involved the regulation of genes related to the LD packaging and TAG degradation without affecting the expression level of transgenes (WRI1, DGAT1, and LEC2) (Supplementary Fig. S7). Oleosins are the most abundant structural proteins that coat the surface of TAG-filled LDs in seeds and pollen to stabilize LDs and prevent TAG turnover, but they are scarcely expressed in tobacco leaf tissue. Unlike the transgene encoding sesame oleosin in HLO, the putative orthologs of N. tabacum encoding Oleosin1 and Oleosin5 were significantly upregulated in HLO under water stress. In contrast, the transcript levels for GDSLs involved in TAG degradation were downregulated. Hence, the main reason for increased TAG accumulation in HLO under WS is likely a combination of reduced degradation and enhanced protection through endogenous gene regulatory networks.

Apart from changes in the regulation of genes involved in TAG metabolism, the expression of transcription factors controlling TAG synthesis was also affected by water stress. WRI1 is a master transcriptional regulator of the plant oil synthesis pathway, and many genes of glycolysis and fatty acid biosynthesis are amongst its targets. In this study, increased expression of WRI1 and its upstream regulators LEC1 and LEC2 under water stress was observed in WT under WS. Whereas, in HLO, only LEC1 was significantly upregulated under WS, and to a much lower level than in WT (Fig. 9). This upregulation of LEC1 and/or LEC2 may contribute to the TAG increase under WS. On the other hand, MYB73 was significantly upregulated in WT under WS (Fig. 9), accompanied by elevated PLDs expression in both genotypes, especially in WT.

In summary, the higher TAG levels in leaves of HLO plants resulted in a trade-off, leading to lower biomass compared to WT. The lower biomass of HLO plants may contribute to lower canopy transpiration, which could improve their performance in water-limited environments. Meanwhile, the HLO plants showed an intrinsic lower unsaturation level of membrane lipids, which help maintain plant function under water stress. Water stress enhanced TAG accumulation in WT and HLO through contrasting mechanisms: WT underwent enhanced lipid remodeling and upregulated genes involved in TAG assembly, LD packaging and downregulated genes related to TAG degradation. In contrast, TAG accumulation in HLO under WS was mainly through upregulating LDs related proteins, i.e. oleosin and downregulating TAG degradation lipase i.e. GDSLs. In addition, transcription factors related to oil synthesis were upregulated by water stress to promote TAG accumulation in both genotypes. Despite the biomass trade-off of the HLO plants, this study demonstrates the efficacy of HLO tobacco technology for oil production in vegetative tissue under moderate to severe water deficit. Such conditions, commonly encountered in field environments, could further promote TAG accumulation compared to well-watered environments. Finally, further research regarding HLO technology should focus on maximizing oil yield under field conditions with abiotic stresses or input limitations (i.e. fertilizers) to assess the real value proposition of this approach for sustainable biofuel production.
Materials and methods
Plant material and growth conditions

The WT tobacco plants, N. tabacum L. cv. Wisconsin 38, and its homozygous transgenic derivative HLO co-expressing four genes including A. thaliana WRI1, DGAT1, LEC2, and S. indicum Oleosin were used in this experiment. Seeds were first germinated on Petri dishes in the dark for 8 days, after which they were transferred to plastic trays filled with a commercial Debco potting mix and placed under natural light in the glasshouse with a 24/16  C light/dark temperature regime. Thirty-eight days after sowing (DAS), 12 seedlings per genotype were transferred to one 1 m3 Nally MegaBin Pallet bins filled with 120 L of gravel at the bottom and a 619 L soil mixture composed of equal parts of composted soil and washed river sand supplemented with 669 grams of Aboska fertilizer (N:P:K at 14.2:6.4:5.1, w:w:w).
Watering management

Soil water relations (i.e. air-filled porosity and gravimetric water content:thetag) were determined according to before the experiment. Bins were watered to saturation with 113 L of tap water (evidenced by drainage after 24 h) before seedling transplantation. After seedling establishment, all the bins were maintained well-watered until 55 DAS when 2 water treatments were imposed was shown in Fig. 1. Each genotype was grown in 4 bins, with 12 plants per bin, under both WW and WS conditions, for a total of 16 bins. The bin layout was randomized. The change of bin weight was logged every 15 min using lysimeters (Accuweigh A500 platform scales, w4 load cells) installed underneath the bins (1 and 2 bins for well-watered (WW) treatment and water-stressed treatment (WS) per genotype, respectively). In the WW treatment, bins were watered daily or every second day with 5-15 L water to maintain bin capacity. In the WS treatment, water was withheld for 23 days, and subsequently rewatered by pumping 2.5 L of water per day (half of the daily soil evaporation) using a buried irrigation system at 15 cm depth.

To assess the severity of water stress, stomatal conductance of new and fully expanded leaves (always the fourth leaf from the top on the main stem) was measured, between 7:30 Am and 9:30 Am AEDT (Australian Easter Daylight Time) with an SC-1leaf porometer (METER group, Pullman, WA, USA) for three plants per bin.
Plant and sample harvest

Leaf tissues and whole plants from each bin were harvested at different stages of development: Vegetative (57 DAS, H1), Elongation (71 DAS, H2), Flowering (78 DAS, H3), and Podding (92 DAS, H4) (Fig. 1). The sample harvesting was conducted during 9:00-10:00 Am for each harvest. Leaf tissues were sampled from leaves at different positions of the plant, i.e. top (young), middle (mature), and bottom (old) of the canopy using a leaf puncher before removing the plant from the bin. Leaf tissues from the same position in corresponding leaves of three plants from 1 bin were pooled and flash frozen in liquid nitrogen as 1 biological replicate. These samples were used for biochemical and transcriptomic analysis. Subsequently, leaves and stems (including buds/pods) were dried at 70  C for 96 h before determining dry weight.
Biochemical analysis

Lipids and carbohydrates extraction: Total leaf lipids were extracted as described in. Briefly, 30 mg of freeze-dried leaf tissue was placed in a 2 mL Eppendorf tube and ground with 2 glass beads using Reich tissue lyser (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) for 3 min at 25 frequency/s. Thereafter, 600 microL of a mixture of chloroform: methanol (2:1, v:v) and 300 microL 0.1 m KCl were added and ground for 3 min at 25 frequency/s, separately. The homogenate was centrifuged, and the lower phase, solid interphase and upper phase were separated for the determination of lipids, starch, and soluble sugars, respectively.

Lipid quantification and fatty acid profiling: TAG was separated from the total lipids by thin layer chromatography (TLC) separation. The amount and fatty acid profile of TFA and TAG were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) with tri-C17:0-TAG as the internal standard as previously detailed.

Starch and sugar quantification: For starch determination, the interphase pellet was resuspended in 350 microL 0.2 m NaOH, boiled for 30 min and neutralized using 3.5 microL glacial acetic acid. The starch content of duplicate 100 microL aliquots was determined relative to a control/blank aliquot using a Megazyme Total Starch Kit (Megazyme International, Ireland). For total soluble sugars determination, aliquots of the upper phase were boiled in anthrone reagent (0.2% anthrone in 70% concentrated H2SO4) for 10 min and the absorbance was measured at 630 nm.
Total carbon determination: Total C was determined from freeze-dried leaf tissue by mass spectrometry (MS) as described in.

Lipid profiling with LC-MS: In order to determine the membrane lipid profiling by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), total lipids of the same leaf samples used in the GC method were extracted from freeze-dried leaf tissue according to. Briefly, 400 microL of cold isopropanol with 0.01% butylated hydroxy toluene were added to each Eppendorf tube containing leaf samples (~30 mg) and cryomilled with Reich tissue lyser (Qiagen). Then the tubes were shaken with preheated thermal shaker (TS-100, BioSan, Riga, Latvia) at 1,400 rpm at 75  C for 15min and cooled to room temperature. Thereafter, 1,200 microL of a mixture of chloroform:methanol:water (30:41.5:3.5, v:v:v) was added to each tube. The tubes were shaken for 24 h at 300 rpm at 25  C and centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 15 min at room temperature. The bottom phase was transferred to a 2 mL Eppendorf tube and dried using the Speedvac concentrator model DNA120-230 (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The dry pellet was reconstituted in 200 muL of butanol:methanol (1:1, v:v) with 10 mm ammonium formate for lipids analysis by LC-MS according to. Selected polar lipids (including PC, PE, PG, MGDG, and DGDG) were analyzed by multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) using a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (Shimadzu LC-MS 8050). Peak areas for each lipid were determined using Lab Solutions Insite (Shimadzu). Quantification of polar lipids was based on external standards 14:0/17:1-PC, 14:0/17:1-PE, 16:0/18:1-PG, 18:3/18:3-MGDG, and 16:0/18:3-DGDG run in the same batch.
RNA-Seq analysis

Total RNA was extracted from middle leaf tissue at H3 with three biological replicates using a Maxwell RSC Plant RNA Kit (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) according to the manufacturer's protocol. The RNA concentration was determined by a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). The RNA quality was assessed with Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies, Waldbronn, Germany) and agarose gel electrophoresis. Thereafter, oligo(dT) magnetic beads were used to enrich the mRNA which was fragmented using divalent cations under elevated temperature in an Illumina proprietary fragment buffer (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). The first-strand cDNA was synthesized by random oligonucleotides and SuperScript II (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with mRNA fragments as the template. Subsequently, second-strand cDNA synthesis was performed using DNA Polymerase I and RNase H. The cDNA libraries were constructed, purified, and sequenced on the Illumina Hiseq platform by Shanghai Personal Biotechnology Co. Ltd (Shanghai, China). One hundred and fifty bp paired-end reads were generated, which were filtered by removing the reads with adapters at the 3' end and low quality (<Q20). After stringent quality assessment and data filtering, clean reads were mapped to the reference genome of N. tabacum (https://solgenomics.sgn.cornell.edu/organism/Nicotiana_tabacum/genome) by HISAT2 software (http://ccb.jhu.edu/software/hisat2/index.shtml).

The differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between WW and WS were determined by P < 0.05 and llog2foldchangel > 1 using DEseq R package (http://www.r-project.org/). To identify the mechanism behind the TAG accumulation under water stress, the genes involved in TAG metabolism and carbohydrate metabolism were screened out for further analysis. For the samples with 4 biological replicates, the observation with the most extreme value based on distance from the mean was removed from the dataset, before statistical analysis, for each isoform by treatment combination. The value of fragments per kilobase per million mapped reads (FPKM) for a gene of interest was transformed via the transformation Y = log2(1 + FPKM) before analysis to stabilize the variance. Transformed FPKM data were analyzed using a two-way factorial structure, water stress treatment by genotype-gene-isoform combination using the R package asreml 4.1.0 running under R 4.0.4. Pairwise treatment contrasts for each genotype-gene-isoform combination were constructed using the R package asremlPlus 4.2-32. Contrast P-values were then converted to false discovery rate (FDR) q-values using the R "p.adjust" function. The significance of the gene expression difference between WW and WS for both genotypes was determined by the FDR q-value <= 0.01 and llog2foldchangel > 1. Analyses of Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) were performed to identify the enrichment of DEGs between WT and HLO in metabolic pathways. The top 20 significantly enriched pathways (FDR <= 0.01) were selected. The ratio between the number of enriched DEGs and all annotated genes in one pathway was shown as a rich factor.
Statistical analysis

One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and student's t-test were used to assess differences in biomass and biochemical parameters between WW and WS for each genotype or between two genotypes under WW conditions. All statistical analyses were performed using the ggplot2 package and VennDiagram package, running under R 4.2.3 (http://www.r-project.org/).

passages.text: All intrinsically active Erk1/2 mutants autophosphorylate threonine207/188, a plausible regulator of the TEY motif phosphorylation

The extracellular-activated kinases 1 & 2 (Erk1/2) are catalytically active when dually phosphorylated on a TEY motif located at the activation loop. In human patients with cardiac hypertrophy, Erk1/2 are phosphorylated on yet another activation loop's residue, T207/188. Intrinsically active variants of Erk1/2, mutated at R84/65, are also (auto)phosphorylated on T207/188. It is not known whether T207/188 phosphorylation is restricted to these cases, nor how it affects Erks' activity. We report that T207/188 phosphorylation is not rare, as we found that: 1) All known auto-activated Erk1/2 variants are phosphorylated on T207/188. 2) It occurs in various cell lines and mouse tissues. 3) It is extremely high in patients with skeletal muscle atrophies or myopathies. We propose that T207/188 controls the permissiveness of the TEY motif for phosphorylation because T207/188-mutated Erk1/2 and the yeast Erk/Mpk1 were efficiently dually phosphorylated when expressed in HEK293 or yeast cells, respectively. The T207/188-mutated Mpk1 was not TEY-phosphorylated in cells knocked out for MEKs, suggesting that its enhanced phosphorylation in wild-type cells is MEK-dependent. Thus, as T207/188-mutated Erk1/2 and Mpk1 recruit MEKs, the role of T207/188 is to impede MEKs' ability to phosphorylate Erks. T207/188 also impedes autophosphorylation as recombinant Erk2 mutated at T188 is spontaneously autophosphorylated, although exclusively on Y185. The role of T207/188 in regulating activation loop phosphorylation may be common to most Ser/Thr kinases, as 86% of them (in the human kinome) possess T207/188 orthologs, and 160 of them were already reported to be phosphorylated on this residue.

Eukaryotic protein kinases (EPKs) modify properties of numerous proteins via reversible phosphorylations and are thereby involved in regulating all physiological processes. EPKs reside in an equilibrium between several conformations, most prominent of which seem to be active and inactive. For most EPKs, the equilibrium is shifted towards the active conformation upon phosphorylation of a particular residue (in Ser/Thr kinases, it is commonly a threonine) within a domain known as the activation loop. This phosphorylation induces an array of new intra-protein interactions that culminate in the assembly of imaginary transverse spines, termed the regulatory and the catalytic spines. The catalytic spine is completed once ATP is bound, stabilizing the active conformation. In many EPKs, activation loop phosphorylation can occur via a spontaneous intrinsic reaction, autophosphorylation, whose mechanism is not fully understood. It is further not clear what is the basis for the more efficient autophosphorylation of some EPKs and the poor autophosphorylation of others.

Thr188 is located in the vicinity of critical residues within the crystal structure of non-phosphorylated Erk2. The structure of inactive human Erk2 (PDB:4S31) is shown in a ribbon representation mode. Position of significant domains and residues is marked.

This study addresses the role of another conserved threonine residue (T197 in PKA, T207/188 in Erk1/2), residing very close to the "activatory" threonine (Fig. 1). This threonine was already noticed by several investigators to be important for catalysis, and to be itself phosphorylated in many EPKs (Table S1). But its exact role and the effect of its phosphorylation have remained unclear. This threonine (will be termed from now on T207/188, on the basis of Erk1/2 numerations) is not required for assembly of the spines, or the active conformation. But, in most EPKs it interacts with a critical Asp, which functions as an activator of substrates' hydroxyls rendering them nucleophilic, capable of attacking ATP. This Asp (D147 in Erk2) is termed, therefore, the catalytic Asp residue (Fig. 1). T207/188 also interacts with a Lys residue of the active site (Lys149; Fig. 1), a single link from the C lobe to phosphate of ATP, which is essential for phosphoryl transfer in many Ser/Thr kinases. Deciphering the role of T207/188 phosphorylation is far from trivial because of three major reasons. First, although this site was found phosphorylated in many EPKs in various cell types and tissues (Table S1), for no EPK it is known how to induce this phosphorylation. Second, because it is not known how to obtain kinases phosphorylated in this residue, one cannot measure its impact on either structure or activity. Third, studying this phosphoacceptor via mutagenesis is futile because mutating this threonine was shown, in a large number of kinases, to impair catalytic capabilities altogether (see Table 1; see also in).

All currently known intrinsically active mutants of Erk1/2 autophosphorylate T207/188 when expressed in E. coli or in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Samples were removed from the cultures at the indicated timepoints post-induction, and cell lysates were prepared and analyzed by Western blot with the indicated antibodies. Cultures were grown to logarithmic phase on YNB(-URA), cell lysates were prepared and analyzed by Western blot with the indicated antibodies. Experiments were performed twice with similar results.
